Facts were re-verified against the primary pages on 2026-10-11.
selected_topic: Would you trust a robot home alone? What home humanoids have actually shown
verified_facts: Figure (Sept 17, 2026): Helix 2.5 was tested in 30 Bay Area homes with no data collected in any of them, on three chores: tidying a living room, folding towels and making a bed.
Figure: the robot completed the entire task in 56% of zero-shot trials (9% for a policy trained from scratch). No partial credit; a safety intervention counted as a failure.
Figure: 'zero-shot' refers to the homes and the objects handled; the chores were specified with fine-tuning data collected elsewhere.
Figure: Helix 2.5 self-corrects, stepping back to reposition, changing stance or moving around a bed to fix a fold.
1X NEO page: 'NEO works autonomously by default. For any chore it doesn't know, you can schedule a 1X Expert to guide it'; the Expert can remotely supervise its actions at scheduled times.

1X (Oct 28, 2025): NEO pre-orders at $20,000 Early Access or $499/month, first orders shipping to homes in 2026; from day one it opens doors, fetches items and turns off lights, and learns more skills over time.
can_do_today: In Figure's own test, a humanoid finished whole household chores in unfamiliar homes about half the time. 1X sells NEO with optional remote human help for chores it doesn't know.
limitations: Figure's 56% comes from Figure's own evaluation, not an independent test.
'Never seen' applies to the homes and objects; the three chores were trained on data collected elsewhere.
1X says NEO works autonomously by default; the remote 1X Expert is scheduled for chores NEO doesn't know.
Figure's robot and 1X's NEO are different robots from different companies; the robot in this reel is an illustration of neither.
speculative: When home humanoids will be reliable enough to leave unsupervised.
Whether NEO has reached paying customers yet (1X says 2026 deliveries; not independently confirmed).
How often NEO owners will need the remote Expert.

hooks.text: Would you leave THIS robot home alone?
This robot finished the job in 56% of homes.
Hate folding laundry? A robot just did it in strangers' homes.
Home robots are coming. Who's watching through their eyes?
The impressive part isn't the folding. It's the retry.

human_story.surprise: Home robots can now do chores in homes they've never seen, but not every time, and one of them can hand the controls to a remote human.
human_story.who_is_affected: Anyone who has imagined coming home to the chores already done.
human_story.why_care: 'Home alone' is the real promise, and it depends on reliability and on who else is in the loop.
human_story.everyday_situation: Walking in the door after work and finding the laundry folded.
human_story.most_compelling_fact: Whole job done in 56% of tries, in Figure's own 30-home test.
human_story.viewer_question: Would I trust it alone in my home, and is it ever really alone?
human_story.scroll_stop_visual: A humanoid robot snapping a towel open in a sunlit living room.

everyday_angle: Coming home to chores done, and deciding who you let in to do them.
key_visual_moment: A toy slips from the robot's hand, it steps back, re-grips and finishes the job.
share_reason: Sent with 'would you get one?' The 56% and the remote-human twist give people something to argue about.

winning_hook.text: Would you leave THIS robot home alone?
winning_hook.why: A personal question the reel actually answers; pairs with a robot already mid-chore in frame one.

opening_visual.first_frame: A humanoid robot's hands snap a white towel open over a low walnut coffee table in a sunlit living room; the towel is already in motion in frame one.
opening_visual.action: The robot folds the towel in half by 1.0s and lays it on a stack; the front door behind it swings open at 1.8s and the host steps in at 2.4s.
opening_visual.camera: Low tracking dolly gliding past the coffee table toward the robot's hands from frame one, rising slightly as the door opens.
opening_visual.narration: Would you leave this robot home alone?
opening_visual.why: The robot doing a chore is the hook; the host arrives as the viewer's stand-in, walking in on it.
